one_liner: Rust WebSocket library (Tokio/Compio; HTTP/1.1, /2, /3) that self-reports 2-3% higher echo throughput than uWebSockets.
what_it_does: An RFC 6455 WebSocket client/server crate for Rust. `WebSocketStream<S>` is a futures `Stream` + `Sink` over any AsyncRead/AsyncWrite transport, with a split reader/writer, permessage-deflate (shared, dedicated and windowed modes), correlated Ping/Pong keepalive, a topic pub/sub helper, Axum integration, and WebSocket over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441) and HTTP/3/QUIC (RFC 9220) on either Tokio or Compio. It is not a drop-in for uWebSockets: uWS is a C++ app framework that owns its event loop and calls your handlers, while sockudo-ws is a library you drive from your own async runtime. It is the WebSocket layer of the Sockudo Pusher-compatible server.
how_it_is_fast: It copies uWebSockets' corking: frames collect in a 16 KiB write buffer and go out in one vectored `writev`, and echo replies queued with `feed()` are flushed once per read batch. Server payloads of 8 KiB or more are queued by reference, not copied. Unmasking uses AVX-512/AVX2/SSE2 kernels picked at runtime on x86-64 and an auto-vectorised 64-byte word loop elsewhere. Text is checked by simdutf8 in one incremental pass that fails fast mid-frame, and frames of 125 B or less take a parser fast path whose payloads are `Bytes` views into a 64 KiB receive buffer, with no copy.
when_to_use: Rust services (Tokio or Compio) that terminate many browser or mobile WebSocket connections and want uWS-style corking and pub/sub fan-out without calling C++ through FFI.

Pipelined or bursty traffic with several messages in flight per connection, if you batch with `feed()` + `flush()`. The project's own harness showed about 2-15x the msg/s of tokio-tungstenite at depth 8-32 with 64-256 B messages (2x on one connection, 15x on 32 connections), but these are historical numbers from the older implicit-coalescing API and have not been re-run.
You need WebSocket over HTTP/2 Extended CONNECT or over HTTP/3/QUIC behind the same stream API as HTTP/1.1, including several WebSockets multiplexed on one connection.
Pusher-style realtime backends that need topic pub/sub with sender exclusion and Pusher socket IDs (Sockudo is built on it).
Replacing tokio-tungstenite in an Axum app when you want permessage-deflate modes with shared or windowed compressors, and keepalive that closes on a missed Pong.
when_not_to_use: Choosing it over uWebSockets for raw throughput. The 2-3% edge is self-reported, cannot be reproduced from published code, and is smaller than the ±5% run-to-run noise the project measured in its own harness.

Request/response traffic with one message in flight. The project's audit found it level with tokio-tungstenite there (158k vs 154-157k msg/s at 64 B with 8-32 connections), because syscalls and scheduler hops cost more than the codec.

Connection storms or fan-out to many connections, where the audit says Tokio's work-stealing scheduler, not the codec, is the limit and a thread-per-core runtime wins. On Compio, write coalescing, zero-copy sends and the shared-sink split writer are not implemented.

Conservative production use. It went from v1.0 to v2.1 in nine months and more breaking changes are waiting in Unreleased. Recent fixes include permessage-deflate stream corruption under context takeover (2.1.0), an O(n·k) UTF-8 re-check that let 4.5 MB of fragmented text pin a core for 30 s (2.0.2), and Pongs never flushed on read-only loops, which got clients dropped (2.0.0).

integration.dependencies: Always: bytes, httparse, http, base64, sha1, simdutf8, socket2, parking_lot, pin-project-lite, futures-core/sink. Default features add tokio + tokio-util, flate2 (zlib-rs backend) + libz-rs-sys, and fastrand. Optional: compio 0.19, h2, quinn/h3/h3-quinn + rustls, tokio-uring, axum/hyper, native-tls or tokio-rustls, ring/aws-lc-rs/openssl/sha1_smol, getrandom/rand, mimalloc.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2024, so rustc 1.85 or later. No rust-version is declared and CI uses latest stable. The bundled Autobahn run needs Rust 1.88+. The README's 'Rust 1.82' cannot build it. Nightly is needed only for extra SIMD targets and fuzzing.
integration.platforms: x86-64 (AVX-512/AVX2/SSE2 masking chosen at runtime; no build-time CPU requirement) and aarch64 (NEON) on stable. CI covers only Linux x86-64 and arm64, and the audit ran on macOS arm64. Windows is not documented. arm, LoongArch, PowerPC and s390x SIMD need nightly, with a portable fallback otherwise. io_uring needs Linux 5.10+.
integration.thread_safety: One `WebSocketStream` per connection, owned by one task. `split()` gives a reader and a writer that can live in different tasks. The writer shares the transport through `Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex>` with a spawned control-driver task, so the Tokio transport must be `Send + 'static`. `PubSub` is shared across tasks (sharded topics, parking_lot locks). Compio `next()` is not cancellation-safe.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — uWebSockets is a C++ framework (also behind uWebSockets.js/Bun) that owns the event loop and dispatches to callbacks. sockudo-ws is a Rust crate you drive from Tokio or Compio. Only the concepts carry over: `Config::uws_defaults()`, corking, and uWS/Bun-style pub/sub.

gotchas: `send()` flushes every frame. To get the batching behind the speed claims, use `feed()` and then `flush()` at batch boundaries. This is a recent contract change in Unreleased. On a unified stream, a write waiting on a slow reader does not advance Pong or idle processing, so one stalled peer can block a sequential fan-out loop.
The README's 'lock-free split streams, zero mutex contention' is out of date. The split writer now locks an `Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex>` shared with a per-connection driver task spawned by `split()`.

The `mimalloc` feature sets a `#[global_allocator]` inside the library. That forces mimalloc on your whole binary and clashes with any other global allocator. The `rustls-*` features no longer choose a crypto provider, so you must enable ring or aws-lc-rs on your own rustls dependency.

The repo builds with `-C target-cpu=native` (.cargo/config.toml) and a fat-LTO, codegen-units=1, panic=abort release profile. Dependents do not inherit these settings, so the published numbers may not match your build. Messages completed through the raw protocol API skip UTF-8 validation, and the repo's benchmark-shaped echo server (`examples/wtx_bench_echo.rs`) uses that path.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings (Kitex, rpcx, brpc, SRPC, grpcxx, cmd-stream, Homa, and wtx's gRPC server) are RPC frameworks or transports for service-to-service calls. Pick sockudo-ws when the peer is a browser or any standard WebSocket client and you need pub/sub fan-out on Tokio or Compio. wtx is the nearest Rust sibling and has its own WebSocket implementation, but its catalogued evidence covers gRPC only.
verified_claims_summary: The authors ran the uSockets `load_test` client from denoland/fastwebsockets (one C event loop, text echo with one message in flight per connection) on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X with Linux 6.18. sockudo-ws reached 222-233k msg/s against 217-228k for the uWebSockets v20.64 EchoServer at 512/1024 B and 100/500 connections, 1.02-1.03x. Neither side's compiler or flags are stated, the stated Rust 1.82 cannot build the edition-2024 crate, the sockudo-ws server and the modified cases are unpublished, and the numbers predate v2. Both servers sit near 230k in every case, which suggests (inference, not measured) that the single-threaded load generator is the ceiling.
status_note: Actively developed (commits through 2026-09-26; v2.1.0 on crates.io with about 116k downloads; reverse dependencies include the Sockudo server crates and nautilus-network) and MIT-licensed. API churn is high and more breaking changes are waiting, so pin the version.
